description: Astral Sentinels es un equipo de estudiantes de Medellín con formación en física, ingeniería mecatronica, matemáticas, ciencia de datos e ingeniería de sistemas. Integramos modelado matemático, métodos numéricos, análisis estadístico y desarrollo de software para abordar problemas científicos. Buscamos crear prototipos funcionales y reproducibles, con énfasis en la interpretación física y la validación de resultados.
summary: KRONOX is a bilingual, browser-based astronomy experience that brings together a 3D Solar System, an immersive all-sky atlas, and a scientific explorer for public SPHEREx observations. Users can travel among planets and moons, adjust simulation time and scale, and pilot a spacecraft. In the atlas, they navigate real HiPS surveys—AllWISE, 2MASS, DSS2, and SPHEREx DR1—overlay survey layers, and inspect Gaia DR3 sources. The SPHEREx explorer covers near-infrared observations from about 0.75 to 5 micrometers and lets users browse its 102-channel sky cube, search targets or coordinates, inspect FITS images, and compare observations using WCS alignment when available. Users can record image notes and export them to CSV. KRONOX combines real public archive data with interactive visualization to make astronomy easier to explore and teach. It was built with React, JavaScript, Three.js, WebGL, Aladin Lite, and Vite, with live data access through NASA/IPAC IRSA and GAVO TAP. Visual scales, false colors, overlays, and the procedural Milky Way are for education and exploration; they are not calibrated scientific measurements.
details:
Overview

KRONOX is a bilingual, browser-based astronomy experience that connects a navigable 3D Solar System, an immersive all-sky atlas, and a scientific explorer for public SPHEREx observations. It is designed to make several different kinds of astronomical information approachable in one place: planetary facts and motion, wide-field sky surveys, star-catalog positions, and infrared image data. The interface guides users from visual exploration toward direct inspection of real archive products while identifying which views are educational visualizations and which come from observational data.

Solar System exploration and spacecraft navigation

The 3D experience is built with React, Three.js, and WebGL. Users can orbit and zoom the scene, change the simulation date and speed, adjust physical and display scales, and move among the Sun, planets, moons, dwarf planets, and points of interest. A spacecraft provides a more embodied way to explore: users can enter its cockpit, choose a destination, plan a manual or automatic trip, or take control at the forward window. Keyboard and touch controls support movement, steering, vertical motion, and temporary acceleration. Planet information panels link to NASA references. Interface language, display quality, contrast, reduced-motion preferences, and optional synthesized sound help accommodate different users and devices.

SPHEREx infrared research

The scientific explorer brings public NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) SPHEREx data into KRONOX. SPHEREx observes the sky in near-infrared light across approximately 0.75 to 5 micrometers. Its six detector bands are represented through a 102-channel spectral view, allowing users to move through the available wavelength channels and inspect sky maps and image data. The atlas notes that channels 51 and 52 are unavailable in the cited release and leaves them blank rather than inventing or interpolating measurements.

Finding and comparing observations

Users can search for a named target or enter ICRS right ascension and declination, review matching observations, filter by detector or band, and browse the observation sequence. The application queries the IRSA Simple Image Access service and retrieves compact image cutouts through IRSA services; local sample FITS products are also included for selected targets. FITS viewers expose the image content for inspection. When two observation dates are compared, KRONOX reads World Coordinate System (WCS) information from the FITS headers and reprojects the images onto a shared sky grid when the available metadata support it. CD/PC matrices and SIP distortion terms are handled when present. A consistent display stretch and celestial grid help users compare source positions; markers and notes can be exported as CSV for later review.

Immersive all-sky atlas

The atlas uses Aladin Lite v3 to navigate real, multiresolution HiPS sky surveys in the browser. Users can switch among AllWISE infrared, 2MASS near-infrared, DSS2 optical, and the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky cube. They can move around the sky, change projections, inspect coordinates and selected objects, and adjust the SPHEREx channel. Layers can be overlaid to compare the appearance of the same region across surveys. Gaia DR3 sources can be queried for the current field through the GAVO TAP service and displayed with catalogue information such as position, magnitude, and parallax.

Region analysis and time views

For selected sky regions, the atlas connects the sky position to the scientific explorer and available SPHEREx coverage. Its analysis panel can display image and WCS-mask thumbnails, inspect temporal differences, and animate observations through time or by channel and detector. The project also includes tools for comparing 64-dimensional representation vectors with cosine similarity or K-nearest-neighbor settings. These are exploratory ways to find similar patterns in the supplied representations; they are not official NASA classifications, chemical identifications, or calibrated scientific conclusions.

How the system is built

The front end uses React, JavaScript modules, JSX, CSS, Three.js, WebGL, and Vite. The Solar System scene, user interface, planetary data, and FITS/WCS utilities are organized as separate modules. Vercel Functions provide server-side access to IRSA search and cutout services and other application endpoints. The atlas loads Aladin Lite and HiPS surveys, while Gaia catalogue queries use GAVO TAP. This design combines a responsive visual client with remote public archives and small local demonstration datasets. Network connectivity is required for live archive queries and some externally hosted resources.

Benefits, intended impact, and scientific scope

KRONOX is intended for students, educators, and curious members of the public who want to explore astronomy interactively. It combines an intuitive sense of place from the 3D scene with direct access to public infrared observations and familiar sky-survey layers. The project emphasizes data provenance, bilingual access, mobile controls, and clear explanations of visual limitations so users can distinguish a compelling display from a scientific measurement. The orbital motion, visual distances, procedural Milky Way, false-color composites, and overlays are simplified or transformed for exploration. HiPS tiles and rendered color do not provide photometry; image reprojection supports visual comparison but is not a substitute for calibration or scientific analysis. Users are directed to the underlying NASA/IPAC IRSA and catalogue sources for research-grade work.
